Where the salt wind strips the scrub down to white bone, the mason knelt in the shale and mortared a low half-ring of river rock around the seep, leaving the south lip open to the trail so mules and strangers could drink without asking.
At dusk the drovers rinsed their tin cups in the overflow trough before dipping from the center, and each morning the basin stood clear again, reflecting the first pale strip of sky.

After an autumn dust-blow left red silt on the bottom step, the mason hung a woven reed lattice across the south gap and began asking each traveler where they had slept the night before before lifting the latch.
By winter he had carved three rules into the lintel—no iron canteens, no dusty hems, and no drawing water after the bell—turning back an old herder whose goats smelled of the lower marsh.

Convinced that even human breath troubled the surface, he laid dressed yellow blocks across the doorway from within, leaving only a thumb-wide slit near the roof to watch the silver skin of the water lie motionless.

Outside, dry hooves scraped against the mortar in the heat and moved on; inside the cool dark, the mason wiped a single speck of lime from the rim and whispered how faithfully he had kept the gift unspoiled.

Because no warm hands dipped into the basin and no overflow ran down the spillway, the dead-still water froze solid to the bedrock on the first black frost, expanding silently against the mortared seams.

At dawn the yellow wall split from footing to crown with a single dry crack, and by noon the thawing meltwater was braiding freely through the rubble into the thorn-grass where three stray kids stood drinking.
At daybreak the stone bakehouse by the pier stood open to the salt wind, and wet deckhands shared warm rye loaves beside the brick oven.

By November the clerk bolted an iron shutter across the oven window and demanded a stamped copper tally before anyone could stand near the heat, leaving shivering net-menders outside on the sleet-slick planks.
Outside, frozen boots shuffled past the shuttered brickwork in the sleet; inside the quiet room, the baker brushed a single pinch of flour from his apron and aligned the brass weights on the shelf.

When the overheated flue latch finally snapped and flung the iron shutter wide, warm cedar smoke and fresh loaves poured onto the wharf; the shivering net-menders gathered close to eat while the baker sat quietly by the open threshold.
